blocking.issue: This regression comes from the fix for the earlier L4S-1. Every undeclared username now shares one bucket, and that makes the status code reveal which usernames exist. An attacker keeps the shared bucket empty by sending about 1 attempt per second with random bogus usernames. Each candidate username is then probed with one wrong password. An undeclared name waits on the empty shared bucket and gets 429 RZ-AUTH-007. A declared name draws from its own full bucket, is hashed, and gets 401 RZ-AUTH-002. So 401 versus 429 tells the attacker whether a username exists, and probing undeclared names costs them nothing. The document claims the opposite. It is also silent on what a new username receives once the 100-per-second bucket-creation limit is reached, which could be a second oracle.
blocking.evidence: Line 403: "| Unknown usernames | One shared bucket and a dummy hash through the same queue, so timing reveals nothing |". Line 405: "created only after the hash queue admits an attempt, at most 100 per second per Node (target)". Line 406: "An empty bucket holds at most 2 waiters, 1,024 per Node, for up to 2 s (target); others get RZ-AUTH-007 with `Retry-After` at once".
blocking.fix: Remove the shared bucket. Give every presented username, declared or not, its own bucket in the same 64-shard LRU, keyed by HMAC-SHA-256 of the username under the per-process key. The 100-per-second creation limit (target) and the hash queue already bound memory and CPU, so the shared bucket is no longer needed. At the creation limit, answer declared and undeclared names the same way (429 RZ-AUTH-007 before any hash). Replace "so timing reveals nothing" with "so neither timing nor status reveals whether a username exists". If the shared bucket stays, state the enumeration residual in T1 and OQ-security-and-identity-15 instead.

blocking.section: Revocation (Expiry); Authentication (JWT and OIDC); Threat model (T2)
blocking.issue: This regression comes from the fix for the earlier L4S-3. A (issuer, kid) revocation entry now expires after the maximum token lifetime, the same as `jti` entries and subject cut-offs. That expiry suits tokens, not keys. Whoever holds a leaked IdP signing key can sign new tokens at any time, each with a fresh `iat` and an `exp` inside the 24-hour bound. If the IdP still publishes that kid in its JWKS when the entry expires, or publishes it again (slow IdP rotation, a stale IdP replica, a restored IdP backup), Nodes accept the leaked key again with no alert. T2 says the leaked key is mitigated by `kid` revocation, but the fix lasts only 24 hours (target).
blocking.evidence: Line 426: "A `jti` entry MUST carry the token's `exp`, capped at the maximum lifetime, and expires then; cut-offs and `kid` entries expire after that lifetime". Line 417: "an IdP key by (issuer, `kid`), forcing a JWKS refetch". Line 91: "| T2 | JWT forgery, leaked IdP key | TB-1, TB-10 | [JWT and OIDC](#jwt-and-oidc); `kid` [revocation](#revocation) |".
blocking.fix: Keep a `kid` entry until an operator removes it. Collect it automatically only after the kid has been missing from every fetched JWKS of that issuer for at least the 6-hour key clamp plus the maximum token lifetime (target). While the entry exists and a JWKS still serves the kid, report a degraded state and emit `credential.revoked` on collection. Count `kid` entries against the 100,000 cap (target) separately so a cap overflow can never displace them. Mark the T2 mitigation as pending OQ-security-and-identity-4.

blocking.section: Control plane security (Admin ports); Threat model (T14)
blocking.issue: This regression comes from the fix for the earlier L4S-7, and it contradicts the foundation pack section 8.4 and System overview TB-9. The new text requires a token only for scraping from off loopback, so `/metrics` over loopback needs no credential. On Kubernetes every container in a Pod shares loopback. That includes the loopback `ollama` sidecar that Secrets rule 6 allowlists and any injected mesh or logging sidecar. A compromised sidecar can therefore read `/metrics` from 9901 and 9902 with no credential, which reveals Route, Upstream, Consumer and error-rate data. The text also does not say what `/metrics` does when no metrics token is configured.
blocking.evidence: Line 480: "Tokens are compared in constant time, only over TLS or loopback; without the operator token, `/tap`, `/config/dump` and `/debug/*` are off, and off-loopback scraping needs a token." Pack section 8.4, 9901 row: "Only `/healthz` and `/readyz` MAY be unauthenticated". System overview TB-9: "the rest MUST require a token or mTLS".
blocking.fix: State that `/metrics` needs the metrics token, the operator token or an admitted client certificate on every interface, loopback included. If no admin credential is configured, only `/healthz` and `/readyz` answer and every other path returns 401. Add sidecar access over shared loopback to T14. If unauthenticated loopback scraping is intended, record it as a proposed amendment to pack 8.4 and TB-9 in OQ-security-and-identity-7, with the residual stated.

non_blocking.suggestion: Scope the client certificates that the `RURALZ_ADMIN_TLS_DIR` CA admits. If they get operator scope, a stolen Prometheus mTLS scraper certificate reaches `/tap` and `/config/dump`, which is the same theft path the metrics token split closed (T14). Give certificates metrics-only scope unless they come from a separate operator CA or carry a marked SAN.

State the capacity for legitimate traffic. With max(1, GOMAXPROCS/4) slots at 10 to 20 verifications per second each, a 16-core Node checks about 40 to 80 credentials per second (hypothesis). With a 60 s success-cache TTL, that serves roughly 2,400 to 4,800 distinct active basic credentials per Node (hypothesis). Flushing the whole cache on every revocation-sequence advance, including unrelated `jti` entries, makes every active basic client re-hash at once. Flush only entries whose username was revoked (store the username HMAC next to the entry). Consider reserving part of the slots for usernames with a recent success, so an anonymous spray cannot take every slot.

Rule 6 misses some cloud metadata addresses: 100.100.100.200 (Alibaba Cloud) and 192.0.0.192 (Oracle Cloud classic). Add them. Add the Kubernetes service-account token path (/var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount) to the rule 5 start-up refusal list, because it is the Vault credential under Kubernetes auth and the credential of the `kubernetes` provider.

A non-loopback State Store URL with credentials but no TLS sends the Redis AUTH secret in cleartext. Anyone on the path can then tamper with entries, which reopens T10 for GCRA and Quota state that the entry MAC does not cover. Refuse readiness in that case, or name it as its own degraded state with its own metric, and link it to OQ-security-and-identity-29.

State how the Node handles four JWT cases: a token without `kid`, where every key of the issuer is tried and counted against the refresh limit; a key's `alg` must match its `kty`, so RS256 and PS256 cannot be swapped on one RSA key; a JWKS key's `use` and `alg` members; and token-type confusion, where an ID token is presented where an access token is expected under a shared audience (`typ` check under OQ-security-and-identity-1).
Say what a new username receives when bucket creation reaches 100 per second per Node (target), and make that response the same for declared and undeclared names.
